title: Blindness in cave animals results from disuse

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Blindness in cave animals results from disuse

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Because useless eyes are unlikely to be harmful in total darkness, the loss of eyes in most cave-dwelling animals is due to disuse alone rather than to natural selection.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: As it is difficult to imagine that eyes, though useless, could be in any way injurious to animals living in darkness, I attribute their loss wholly to disuse.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter V, “Laws of Variation”; section “Use and disuse, combined with natural selection; organs of flight and of vision.”. Scope: cave-dwelling animals

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch05-05: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.63

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Modern cave systems have unusually rich genomic and developmental data that can strongly test exclusivity. They cannot recover every historical step or generalize to most cave-dwelling animals.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Across independent cave lineages, estimate fitness costs of eyes, molecular signatures of relaxed versus positive selection, and developmental mechanisms of eye reduction. Positive selection for eye loss or measurable energetic and pleiotropic costs would refute loss by disuse alone.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Relaxed selection, drift and adaptive energy savings can leave overlapping signatures.

The historical category 'disuse alone' is not a single modern mechanism.

fields.value:

discriminating power: 0.61

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The claim names a cause, disuse alone, and explicitly sets selection aside, so molecular signatures of selection are relevant in principle. Those signatures are public for a small set of cave species and absent for most of the scope. Where genomes exist, the analysis can challenge the exclusion of selection without measuring disuse directly.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: In cave lineages with sequenced eye-loss genes, test for relaxed constraint, positive selection, or pleiotropy with other cave phenotypes. Neutral loss independent of selection would support a disuse-or-drift reading; repeated signatures of selection or pleiotropic benefit would refute the claim that eyes were lost wholly without selection. Mapping disuse onto neutral degeneration is an interpretive step.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Pleiotropy can look like selection on eyes when selection acted on a linked trait.

Disuse, as inheritance of an acquired loss, is not a variable in sequence data.

Genetic tests exist for a few models, especially Astyanax, not for most cave animals.
